opus-5.5.text:
I think needle-in-a-haystack was a useful first step, but it's a pretty weak proxy for what we actually care about.

What it tests is basically retrieval: you hide one fact somewhere in a very long context, then ask the model to find it. Early long-context models really did fail at this, so as a sanity check it made sense. If a model can't even find the needle, it obviously can't use long context. But once models started scoring close to 100%, it became clear the benchmark was saturated, and passing it doesn't tell you much.

The deeper issue is that real long-term memory isn't "find the one sentence that matches the question." It's more like this: you've worked with someone for three months, and you've built up an understanding of their preferences, their codebase, what they tried that failed, and why some decision was made. Using that memory means integrating lots of scattered pieces, knowing what's relevant without being told, handling information that's been updated or contradicted, and forgetting what doesn't matter. None of that is captured by a single needle with a lexically obvious query.

So I'd say needle-in-a-haystack is necessary but far from sufficient. It measures whether the context window "works" mechanically, not whether the model has memory in a meaningful sense.

More broadly, I think evaluation is becoming more important than training methods. We have pretty general recipes now, and the bottleneck is defining tasks that reflect real utility. For memory, a good eval should look like real usage: long-horizon interactions where the model has to accumulate context over time, and success depends on actually using what it learned earlier. That's harder to build and harder to score, but it's much closer to what matters if we want agents that work with people over weeks or months instead of one session at a time.

r001.rationale: It calls needle-in-a-haystack a necessary check, saying that if a model cannot find the needle, it cannot use long context.

r002.rationale: It says the benchmark is a weak proxy and that passing it does not show meaningful long-term memory.

r003.rationale: It criticizes the benchmark as weak and saturated, but does not say long-term-memory evaluation research remains overly focused on needle-style tasks.

r004.rationale: It calls evaluation a bottleneck, but does not say inadequate evaluation makes it difficult to compare the merits of different memory approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
I think needle-in-a-haystack is a useful test, but it's really a test of retrieval, not of memory in the sense that matters.

What it measures is: can the model find a fact that's sitting verbatim somewhere in a very long context? That's basically a search problem. And once labs started optimizing for it, it got saturated pretty quickly — you can get near-perfect scores on it without the model actually being good at using long context. It's a bit like the situation with a lot of benchmarks: the metric was a decent proxy at first, and then it stopped being a proxy once people targeted it directly.

The thing I actually care about is something closer to how an agent uses experience. If you think about a human working on a task for a long time, memory isn't "I can recall any sentence I read in the last three days." It's more like: you accumulate a model of what's going on, you compress it, you forget the irrelevant parts, and you keep the parts that matter for what you're going to do next. So the real question is whether a model can take a very long history of interaction — observations, its own actions, mistakes, feedback — and update its behavior based on that. That involves reasoning over the context, not just locating a string in it.

Needle tests don't capture any of that. There's no interference — the needle is usually unrelated to everything around it, so there's no confusion about which of several similar facts is the right one. There's no need to synthesize across multiple pieces of information. There's no notion of something being true earlier and no longer true later. And most importantly, nothing in the context is the model's own output. In an agent setting, a lot of the context is what the model did — tool calls, intermediate results, failed attempts — and the hard part is learning from that trajectory.

So I'd say: it's fine as a sanity check. If a model fails needle-in-a-haystack, it definitely has a problem. But passing it tells you very little. For evaluating long-term memory, I'd want tasks that are more like long-horizon agentic environments, where the model has to carry state across many steps, where the context contains lots of distractors that look relevant, and where you can measure whether performance actually improves as the history gets longer. If a model with a million tokens of context performs the same as a model with ten thousand on a task where the extra history should help, then the long context isn't really being used as memory, no matter how well it finds needles.

There's also a deeper point, which is that long context and memory may not be the same thing in the end. Context is a mechanism; memory is a capability. You could implement memory with retrieval, with fine-tuning, with some external state the agent writes to. Needle-in-a-haystack only evaluates one mechanism, and I'm not sure it's the one that matters most.

r003.rationale: The response critiques the test’s limits and describes benchmark saturation, but does not say long-term-memory evaluation research remains overly focused on these tasks.

r004.rationale: It says the test evaluates one mechanism, but does not state that inadequate evaluation makes it difficult to compare the merits of different memory approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think needle-in-a-haystack tasks test a useful capability, but a fairly narrow one. You put a piece of information somewhere in a long context and ask the model to retrieve it. If it fails, that tells you something. But if it succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily mean it has good long-term memory.

The key difference is that, in this test, someone has already decided what to keep and put everything into the context. In a long-running system, deciding what to remember is part of the problem. What should you preserve from an interaction? What should you summarize or discard? And when new information contradicts something you remembered, how do you update it?

There’s also a difference between finding an explicitly requested fact and using a memory when nobody tells you to retrieve it. If I told an assistant about a preference last week, ideally it would apply that preference to a relevant task today without my having to say, ‘Remember what I told you last week.’

So I would treat needle-in-a-haystack as a basic retrieval diagnostic. For long-term memory, I’d want to evaluate an agent across a sequence of interactions and see whether its past experience actually improves its later decisions.

r001.rationale: It calls the task a useful basic retrieval diagnostic, but does not say that success is necessary for effective long-term memory.

r002.rationale: It says success does not necessarily mean the model has good long-term memory.

r003.rationale: It describes needle-in-a-haystack as narrow, but does not criticize long-term-memory evaluation research for focusing too heavily on that style of task.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss how evaluation affects comparisons among long-term-memory approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think needle-in-a-haystack is useful, but it measures a fairly narrow capability. You put a piece of information somewhere in a long context and ask the model to retrieve it. That tells you whether the model can find something, but long-term memory requires more than finding a sentence.

For example, if an agent interacts with you for months, what should it remember? What should it forget? If you change your preference, can it update that memory instead of continuing to use the old one? And can it recognize when a past experience is relevant, even when you don’t explicitly ask it to recall that experience?

There’s also a difference between having the entire history available in the context and having to manage memory over time. In the second case, the agent has to decide what to store and how to organize it, often before it knows what questions will come later.

So I’d treat needle-in-a-haystack as a basic diagnostic for long-context retrieval. For long-term memory, I’d rather evaluate whether an agent actually gets better at helping you through repeated interactions, especially when remembering requires combining experiences, updating beliefs, and applying what it learned to a new situation.

r002.rationale: It says the task measures a narrow retrieval capability and that long-term memory requires additional abilities such as deciding what to retain, updating memories, and applying past experiences.

r003.rationale: It describes needle-in-a-haystack as narrow, but does not criticize long-term-memory research for being overly focused on such tasks.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss how evaluation affects comparisons of different long-term-memory approaches.
